summary: A target-level follow-up of the accepted T.1 packet for the classical field presentation. Existing symbol and Milnor targets retain their ids; fifteen new proof inputs specify the homogeneous quotient, field-only sign calculus, root-word normalization, zero-symbol splitting, and the infinite-field Matsumoto extension and completeness proof, unique divisibility, the canonical real positive-entry complement, and a noncircular finite Milnor calculation. Finite classical presentation, arithmetic Bass–Tate proofs and the inherited stable-colimit witness remain explicit gaps.

nodes.title: The degree-two tensor realization
nodes.statement: Set T₂(F)=U⊗ℤU, R₂(F)=spanℤ{a⊗b : a,b∈F× and a+b=1 in F}, and Q₂(F)=T₂(F)/R₂(F). Let symbol(a,b) be the quotient class of a⊗b. For every abelian group A, evaluation on symbols identifies Homℤ(Q₂(F),A) with bilinear maps U×U→A annihilating these complementary-unit tensors.
hypotheses: For any commutative field F, use its multiplicative unit group U=F× written additively as Additive Fˣ; all tensors and spans are over ℤ.
proofSteps: Use the pinned tensor product and Submodule quotient directly. Relations are a submodule of a degree-two module, not an ideal requiring a commutative tensor algebra.
TensorProduct.lift extends a bilinear pairing. It vanishes on the span exactly when it vanishes on each complementary-unit tensor; use Submodule.liftQ to descend it.
Pure tensors generate the tensor product additively; their images generate the quotient. Equality on symbols therefore proves homomorphism extensionality.
A field homomorphism preserves units and complementary-unit equations. The universal property gives the induced map; identity and composition follow by extensionality.
acceptance: The universal property is unique existence, not merely existence of a descended map.
The scalar ring is ℤ; quotienting by squares as well would give a different object.

sources.locator: Definition III.7.1, printed pp.61–62; Theorem III.6.1, printed p.48
sources.match: The degree-two presentation uses bilinearity and complementary entries. The universal-property formulation follows from the pinned quotient and tensor APIs.

nodes.title: The homogeneous Steinberg quotient bridge
nodes.statement: In the inherited tensor-algebra definition of K*M(F), let T_n be the degree-n module. Its relation module R_n is the sum, over i+j=n−2, of images of T_i⊗R₂⊗T_j under concatenation; R₀=R₁=0. Construct canonical equivalences K⁽M⁾_n(F)≅T_n/R_n compatible with concatenation and field maps, including K⁽M⁾₂(F)≅Q₂(F). The natural map from the direct sum of these quotients to the ungraded ring quotient is an additive equivalence.
hypotheses: For any commutative field F, use its multiplicative unit group U=F× written additively as Additive Fˣ; all tensors and spans are over ℤ.
n is a natural number; the generating relations have degree exactly two.
proofSteps: Consume TensorAlgebra.gradedAlgebra; do not construct the tensor-algebra grading again.

Describe the two-sided ideal as finite sums of words p·(a⊗b)·q, with a+b=1. Decompose p and q into their finitely many homogeneous terms; each summand remains in that ideal and has its computed degree.
This proves degree projection preserves the ideal. Its intersection with T_n is precisely R_n, since each word of total degree n has prefix and suffix degrees summing to n−2.
Each graded quotient has a multiplication induced by concatenation: R_iT_j+T_iR_j⊆R_{i+j}. Prove quotient well-definedness before asserting the grading.

The direct-sum map is surjective by finite homogeneous expansion and injective by componentwise ideal membership. Use this equivalence to transport the graded ring structure to the inherited ungraded quotient.
For n=0,1 there are no relation words, giving ℤ and U; for n=2 the prefix and suffix are scalars, giving exactly the tensor realization.
acceptance: No positive-degree relation kills an integer in degree zero.
The multiplication is associative and unital and respects the grading.
The degree-two equivalence sends the inherited Milnor symbol to symbol(a,b), not its inverse.

sources.match: The source defines a homogeneous ideal quotient and describes each degree by multilinear symbols. The component-intersection proof fills in the grading bridge left unstated there.

nodes.title: Field-only proof of the symbol sign identities
nodes.statement: For any bilinear pairing c:F××F×→A into an abelian group with c(a,1−a)=0 for a≠0,1, one has c(a,−a)=0, c(a,b)=−c(b,a), c(a,a)=c(a,−1), and 2c(a,a)=0. In characteristic two c(a,a)=0. The statement applies to the inherited classical symbol and the tensor realization without a general-ring localization theorem.
hypotheses: F is a commutative field; A is an abelian group; c is bilinear in multiplicative units and annihilates complementary units.
proofSteps: Bilinearity gives c(1,b)=c(a,1)=0, inversion identities and 2c(a,−1)=c(a,1)=0.
For a≠1, apply the relation to a⁻¹ and (a−1)/a; expanding gives c(a,a−1)=c(a,a). Apply the relation to a and −(a−1) to get c(a,−1)+c(a,a)=0. This also handles a=1 by normalization.
Thus c(a,−a)=0. Expand c(ab,−ab) using −ab=(−a)b=a(−b), cancel the diagonal-negative terms and obtain c(a,b)+c(b,a)=0.
Since c(a,−1) is killed by two, its negative equals itself, yielding the square formula with the stated sign. In characteristic two −1=1, so the square is zero.
acceptance: No assumption that 1−a is a unit is made when a=1; that case has its own normalization argument.
Over ℝ the square c(−1,−1) need not vanish.
The proof does not use Matsumoto injectivity or residues.

sources.locator: Definition III.7.1, printed p.61; Exercise III.6.3, printed pp.58–59; identity preceding III.6.1, printed p.47

nodes.title: Weyl conjugation and commutator-symbol normalization
nodes.statement: For commutative F and pairwise distinct i,j,k in St_m(F), m≥3, w_ij(r)w_ij(−r)=1, w_ij(r)x_ij(s)w_ij(r)⁻¹=x_ji(−r⁻²s), and w_ij(r)x_ji(s)w_ij(r)⁻¹=x_ij(−r²s). After stabilization, or in a compatible central extension, the inherited commutator convention gives {r,s}=h_ij(rs)h_ij(r)⁻¹h_ij(s)⁻¹=h_ij(r)h_ij(s)h_ij(rs)⁻¹. This fixes the positive normalization when comparing Matsumoto’s cocycle with the classical symbol.
hypotheses: r,s∈F× for torus expressions; the root parameter in conjugation can be any field element; m≥3.
proofSteps: The inverse word follows by reversing the three root generators and negating parameters. For a nonopposite root expand the three conjugations using the ordinary chaining relations; retain the root coefficient order.

For opposite roots choose the third index and express x_ij(s) as [x_ik(s),x_kj(1)]. Conjugate both nonopposite factors and recombine with the chaining relation. This gives the two opposite-root formulas without adding them as relations.
Conjugation by h_ik(r) scales the ij root parameter by r and the ji parameter by r⁻¹. Thus h_ik(r)h_ij(s)h_ik(r)⁻¹=w_ij(rs)w_ij(−r)=h_ij(rs)h_ij(r)⁻¹.

In the stable central extension, taking the commutator gives {r,s}=h_ij(rs)h_ij(r)⁻¹h_ij(s)⁻¹. Swapping r,s and using central skew-symmetry identifies this with h_ij(r)h_ij(s)h_ij(rs)⁻¹. Do not commute two same-root torus lifts without their central correction.
acceptance: The coefficient −r⁻²s is required in the opposite-root conjugation formula.
The two inverse torus factors appear in order r then s; reversing them changes the result in general.
No finite-rank kernel centrality is assumed from the stable centre theorem; the torus-defect equality is asserted stably or in an explicitly central extension.

sources.locator: Exercises III.5.8–5.9, printed p.46, with the torus-factor order corrected; Matsumoto Lemma 5.4(c), printed p.26

nodes.title: The type-A torus factor set for a prescribed symbol
nodes.statement: For infinite F, m≥3, an abelian A and bilinear Steinberg pairing c, index simple roots by 1,…,m−1, α_i=e_i−e_{i+1}. On H=(F×)^(m−1) define C(t,u)=Σ_i c(t_i,u_i)−Σ_{i=2}^{m−1}c(t_i,u_{i−1}). Use the pinned normalized factor-set extension to form H~. Its ordered section is the product of h_i(t_i); the torus image in SL_m is ∏diag_i(t_i,t_i⁻¹), not the tuple interpreted as diagonal entries.
hypotheses: F infinite and commutative; m≥3; A an additive abelian group; c bilinear with the Steinberg relation.
proofSteps: Use Multiplicative A and the trivial H action in TauCeti.FactorSet. Bilinearity of C gives the cocycle equation and C(1,t)=C(t,1)=0.

The Cartan entries for type A are 2 on the diagonal, −1 on adjacent nodes and zero otherwise. The lower adjacent sum records exactly the central correction for reordering the chosen simple-root lifts.
Use the existing factor-set extension injection and centrality theorem. Ordered section multiplication has defect C; the single-root defect is c(a,b).
Convert simple-coroot coordinates to diagonal coordinates: (t₁,t₂/t₁,…,t_{m−1}/t_{m−2},t_{m−1}⁻¹). This is the determinant-one torus.
acceptance: For type A₂ the factor is c(t₁,u₁)+c(t₂,u₂)−c(t₂,u₁).
A is injected, rather than quotiented by an unstated relation.

sources.locator: §6, construction (2)–(3), printed pp.35–37; Lemma 5.4(c), printed pp.26–27
sources.match: The ordered torus extension records the prescribed root-symbol cocycles and Cartan corrections. The formula is its additive type-A specialization.

nodes.title: The symbol-dependent lift of the type-A normalizer
nodes.statement: Extend H~ to N~ over the monomial determinant-one normalizer N⊂SL_m(F), with simple lifts w_i=w_i(−1), root-torus lifts h_i(t), injected central A and kernel A. The action is θ_i⁻¹(h_j(t))=h_j(t)h_i(t^(−⟨α_i,α_j∨⟩)); θ_i fixes A. Its square is conjugation by h_i(−1), the w_i satisfy type-A braid relations, and w_i²=h_i(−1).
hypotheses: The input and conventions of torus-factor-set, with the ordered type-A simple roots.
proofSteps: Consume the ordinary normalizer and Weyl group from ReductiveGroups Layer 7; the coefficient-dependent lifting is new work here.

Verify the stated θ_i⁻¹ preserves torus multiplication, using field-calculus for equal, adjacent and nonadjacent indices. Its square is inner by h_i(−1), not generally the identity on the torus extension.
Form the source semidirect construction with the group of simple normalizer words; identify their square generators with the corresponding h_i(−1). Lemma 6.6 proves this quotient keeps H~ embedded.
Use Lemma 6.5 to verify length-two and length-three braids and the resulting projection onto N. The normalizer kernel is the already injected A. No general Tits-system theory is replanned here.
acceptance: The square relation retains h_i(−1), rather than incorrectly setting w_i²=1.
The coefficient injection stays faithful after the square identifications.

nodes.title: The Bruhat fiber set and its lift action
nodes.statement: Let v:SL_m(F)→N be the unique normalizer coordinate in its upper-unipotent Bruhat double coset, as in Matsumoto Lemma 5.3. Define S={(g,n~):v(g)=q(n~)}. This is a set, with each fiber an A-torsor, and not a fiber-product group; the simple-lift branches test the sign of σ⁻¹α_i and then the simple root coordinate t. Construct permutations λ(h), λ(u), λ(w_i) lifting left multiplication by h∈H, u∈U⁺ and w_i∈N; let E_c be their generated subgroup of Perm(S).
hypotheses: F infinite; m≥3; the symbol-dependent normalizer and the ordinary Bruhat coordinate v are fixed.
proofSteps: Use the ordinary Bruhat coordinate uniqueness and its transformation rules from ReductiveGroups Layer 7, requested with the precise SL_m specialization.
For u∈U⁺ set λ(u)(g,n~)=(ug,n~). For h~∈H~ set λ(h~)(g,n~)=(q(h~)g,h~n~). The transformation rules for v prove these remain in S.

Write g=u₀ x_i(t) v(g) u′, with u₀ in the upper subgroup omitting the simple root α_i and Weyl coordinate σ. If σ⁻¹α_i is positive or t=0, λ(w_i)(g,n~)=(w_i g,w_i n~). If σ⁻¹α_i is negative and t≠0, λ(w_i)(g,n~)=(w_i g,h_i(t⁻¹)n~). Lemma 5.3(d) proves these remain in S; the transformation rules are requested from the ordinary Bruhat owner.
Check each formula has an inverse before generating E_c. Projection on the first coordinate defines a homomorphism E_c→SL_m, because each generating permutation lifts that fixed left multiplication.
Define the opposite right permutations through the inversion involution (g,n~)↦(g⁻¹,n~⁻¹); their commutation with left permutations is the next theorem, not an axiom.
acceptance: S is nonempty over every g since q:N~→N is surjective.
The simple-root zero branch uses no inversion of zero.
A acts on each fiber by central translation.

sources.locator: Lemma 5.3, printed pp.24–25; construction before Lemma 6.8, printed pp.40–41; §7, printed pp.44–45

nodes.title: Rank-one and rank-two verification of the lift action
nodes.statement: In the preceding construction the left and opposite right actions commute. The left lifts obey additive root relations, Weyl conjugation of roots, and all type-A rank-two commutator and braid relations. In particular [x_ij(r),x_jk(s)]=x_ik(rs) and [x_ij(r),x_ki(s)]=x_kj(−sr) for distinct i,j,k. These assertions include the opposite-root conjugation identities used by Bruhat reduction.
hypotheses: The infinite-field construction above; type-A root indices and the prescribed c with its complementary-unit relation.
proofSteps: Reduce to simple-root subgroups and rank-two root subsystems using the ordinary positive-root decomposition. Type A requires only A₁×A₁ and A₂ calculations, not the source symplectic C₂ case.
Use the opposite right action and reduce its commutation with each left generator to representatives x_α(u)w_σx_β(v). Split into σβ≠±α, σβ=α and σβ=−α as in §7.
The first two branches follow from torus conjugation and ordinary root commutators. In the opposite branch separate uv=0, uv=1 and uv(1−uv)≠0, so all reciprocals carry nonzero witnesses.
In the final branch the discrepancy is a central combination of c evaluated at complementary parameters; the Steinberg relation cancels it. This is the essential use of c(a,1−a)=0 beyond bilinearity.
Transitivity of both actions and their commutation make each simply transitive. Apply Lemma 6.9 on subsystem fibers and Lemma 6.10 to obtain the defining lifted relations globally.
acceptance: The root coefficient order is rs forward and −sr in reverse chaining.
The uv=1 branch is checked independently, not by substituting into a formula with (1−uv)⁻¹.
Opposite-root conjugation is proved, rather than inferred solely from Weyl braid relations.

sources.locator: Lemmas 6.8–6.10, printed pp.41–42; proof in §7, printed pp.44–47
sources.match: Commuting opposite actions verify the rank-two relations needed for the lifted Bruhat decomposition and the symbol-realizing extension.

nodes.title: Faithful realization and Bruhat normal form for the symbol extension
nodes.statement: The generated permutation group E_c fits into an exact central extension 0→A→E_c→SL_m(F)→1. Every element admits a lifted Bruhat expression u h~ w_σ v, with v in the root-coordinate subgroup appropriate to σ. The only kernel elements are coefficient translations. A homomorphism St_m(F)→E_c takes elementary root generators to their lift permutations, and the symbol [h_ij(a),h_ik(b)] maps to inl(c(a,b)) for distinct i,j,k.
hypotheses: F infinite and m≥3; the type-A ordinary root presentation and Bruhat form, plus the preceding verified lift action.
proofSteps: Use rank-two-action to show the union of lifted Bruhat cells contains the identity and is stable under left multiplication by every root generator; hence it contains the generated group.
Project a normal form to its ordinary Bruhat expression. If the projection is identity, uniqueness removes the Weyl and unipotent coordinates and leaves precisely the coefficient A.
Coefficient translations inject by their action on (1,1). They commute with every left generator, so kernel identification proves central exactness without an assumption of faithfulness.

The verified elementary relations induce St_m(F)→E_c by its presentation universal property. Match the source cocycle h_α(a)h_α(b)h_α(ab)⁻¹ to the commutator definition: α=e_i−e_j, β=e_i−e_k have pairing +1 in Lemma 5.4(c), giving +c(a,b).
Set A=0 for the presentation-completeness specialization. For arbitrary A, retain the coefficient injection rather than only a surjection onto the desired central subgroup.
acceptance: The coefficient class cannot disappear in the generated permutation group.
Taking A=0 yields SL_m(F).
The source h_α(a)=w_α(a)w_α(1)⁻¹ agrees with inherited w_ij(a)w_ij(−1); verify the rank-one inverse word.

sources.locator: Lemma 6.11, printed pp.42–43; Theorem 5.10 and Corollary 5.11, printed pp.30–31; Lemma 5.4(c), printed pp.26–27
sources.match: Lifted Bruhat reduction identifies the kernel and completes the constructed extension. The commutator-cocycle comparison fixes the sign of the realized symbol.

nodes.title: Stable relation separation for the inherited Matsumoto target
nodes.statement: For infinite F, specialize the preceding construction to A=Q₂(F) and c=the tensor symbol. The canonical map Q₂(F)→K₂(F) is injective: every finite symbol relation that becomes trivial in the stable Steinberg group is already zero in Q₂(F). The lifted normal form also shows every stable kernel element is a finite product of symbols. Together these are proof inputs for the existing Matsumoto isomorphism, not a second definition of it.
hypotheses: F infinite; the stable Steinberg group and its finite-representative equality criterion are supplied by T.1.
proofSteps: A finite symbol expression involves finitely many root indices. If it dies after stabilization, the directed-colimit equality criterion witnesses its vanishing in one sufficiently large St_m(F).

Apply that rank’s faithful-realization with A=Q₂(F). Each commutator symbol maps to its tensor class, so the zero word acts as zero coefficient translation; coefficient injectivity gives the required zero relation.

For generation, let C be the subgroup of stable K₂ generated by all symbols and quotient the stable Steinberg extension by C. It remains central, and its elementary root lifts have zero torus defects by root-word-normalization. Each pullback to SL_m(F), m≥3, splits by zero-symbol-splitting. Perfectness makes the splittings unique, hence compatible on rank inclusions; the inherited stable-colimit universal property gives a stable section. A split central extension with perfect total group has trivial central kernel: its abelian central factor must vanish. The quotient St(F)/C is perfect as a quotient of St(F), so K₂(F)/C=0.

No compatible choices of E_c across all ranks are required for the separation argument: every relation is tested in its witnessing finite rank. Naturality of the resulting isomorphism follows from symbols and the quotient universal property.
This infinite-field argument must not be applied to finite fields. The finite-field classical comparison retains the explicit source gap recorded separately.
acceptance: Injectivity is not justified by merely showing symbol relations hold in classical K₂.
The proof works in a finite witness rank before taking the stable conclusion.
Stabilization preserves the chosen symbol convention.

sources.locator: Corollary 5.11, printed pp.30–31; Lemma 6.11, printed pp.42–43; Weibel Theorem III.6.1, printed p.48
sources.match: The original extension proof supplies the completeness direction for infinite fields. Finite-rank witnesses connect it to the stable kernel target already owned by the predecessor.

nodes.title: Zero-symbol splitting for finite type-A central extensions
nodes.statement: Let F be infinite, m≥3, and E→SL_m(F) a central extension by A with compatible root lifts satisfying the ordinary root and Weyl-conjugation relations. If all its torus-defect cocycles h_i(a)h_i(b)h_i(ab)⁻¹ are trivial, the extension splits. The splitting carrying elementary matrices to these lifts is unique, since SL_m(F) is perfect.
hypotheses: F infinite and commutative, m≥3; the coefficient kernel is central; compatible root lifts are supplied as part of the hypothesis.
proofSteps: By root-word-normalization a zero commutator symbol is a zero simple-root torus defect. No unspecified choice of root sections enters this specialization.

Zero defect makes each h_i:F×→E multiplicative. The root lifts then satisfy the full ordinary group presentation (R1),(R2),(R3) at Matsumoto p.23, supplied as the exact SL_m specialization requested from ReductiveGroups.
The presentation universal property induces a section SL_m→E, agreeing with all root lifts. This is the zero-cocycle/injectivity part of Theorem 5.10, not its construction part.
If two sections exist, their pointwise ratio is a homomorphism SL_m→A because A is central. Elementary matrices are commutators using a third index, so SL_m is perfect; the ratio is trivial.
acceptance: No arbitrary extension is asserted to split; the zero-cocycle hypothesis is essential.
The result applies to restrictions of a central quotient of the stable Steinberg extension, whose root lifts are inherited.

sources.locator: §5 ordinary presentation (R1)–(R3), printed p.23; paragraph preceding Theorem 5.10, printed p.30
sources.match: Trivial symbol cocycles make the root lifts satisfy the full group presentation, giving a splitting; perfectness gives uniqueness.

nodes.title: Divisibility and torsion in tensor quotients
nodes.statement: Let p>0. If abelian groups U,V are p-divisible then multiplication by p on U⊗ℤV is bijective. If multiplication by p on an abelian group T is bijective and its subgroup R is p-divisible, then multiplication by p on T/R is bijective. These statements need no torsion-freeness assumption on U or V themselves.
hypotheses: p a positive integer; U,V,T abelian groups; R an additive subgroup or equivalently an ℤ-submodule of T.
proofSteps: Surjectivity on U⊗V follows by taking a p-preimage in one tensor slot and extending from pure tensors.

Use pinned rTensor_exact on U[p]→U→U→0, where the second arrow is multiplication by p and is surjective. Every tensor of an element killed by p with V vanishes because V is p-divisible; hence multiplication by p on U⊗V is injective. No flatness assumption on divisible groups is made.
For the quotient, surjectivity descends from T. If pt∈R, choose r∈R with pr=pt. Injectivity in T implies t=r, so its quotient class is zero.
Iterate the tensor statement for degrees n≥2; the remaining tensor block stays p-divisible. The relation-subgroup calculation is the separate next input.
acceptance: Divisibility of a quotient alone does not rule out torsion.
Q/ℤ is a counterexample if the subgroup hypothesis is dropped from the quotient claim: ℤ is not p-divisible.

sources.locator: Proposition III.6.4.1, printed p.52; Exercise III.7.3, printed p.72
sources.match: The source tensor and relation-subgroup argument yields unique divisibility; this is the reusable additive statement underlying it.

nodes.title: Root factorization divides the homogeneous relation modules
nodes.statement: For a prime p, assume every polynomial X^p−a with a∈F× splits into linear factors over F. Every relation module R_n from homogeneous-components is p-divisible. For n≥2, multiplication by p on T_n/R_n is bijective. Thus this input proves the inherited unique-divisibility target for algebraically closed fields in exactly degrees n≥2.
hypotheses: F a field, p prime; every X^p−a for a nonzero splits over F; repeated roots are counted with multiplicity.
proofSteps: List all p roots b₁,…,b_p of X^p−a, with multiplicities. None is zero; for a≠1 none is one. Evaluation at 1 gives 1−a=∏(1−b_i).
In T₂, expand a⊗(1−a)=Σ_i a⊗(1−b_i)=pΣ_i b_i⊗(1−b_i), since b_i^p=a. Every summand is a relation. This proves each degree-two generator lies in pR₂, with the reverse inclusion automatic.
Multiply this equality by arbitrary prefix and suffix tensors. The R_n description implies R_n=pR_n in every degree; degrees zero and one have zero relation module.

F× is p-divisible by root existence. Apply tensor-divisibility to T_n for n≥2 and then to its p-divisible relation module. Homogeneous-components transports the resulting bijection to inherited K⁽M⁾_n.

An algebraically closed field satisfies the hypothesis for each prime; compositions of prime multiplications give unique divisibility by every positive integer. Degree one can have roots-of-unity torsion and degree zero is ℤ.
acceptance: In characteristic p, use multiplicities, not a false assertion that there are p distinct roots.
For algebraically closed F, the assertion is n≥2; it does not assert F× is uniquely divisible.

sources.locator: Proposition III.6.4.1, printed p.52; Exercise III.7.3, printed p.72
sources.match: The root factorization gives a p-preimage inside the relation subgroup itself. The same argument with prefixes and suffixes handles all degrees at least two.

nodes.title: The positive-entry subgroup over the real field
nodes.statement: For n≥1 let D_n⊂K⁽M⁾_n(ℝ) be the ℤ-span of symbols with at least one strictly positive entry. Let e_n={−1,…,−1}. Then D_n is divisible, e_n has exact order two, and every class decomposes uniquely as εe_n+d with ε∈ℤ/2 and d∈D_n. The sign map sends a symbol to 1 in ℤ/2 exactly when all entries are negative, and its kernel equals D_n. For n=2 use the light realization realPositive⊂Q₂(ℝ).
hypotheses: n≥1; the usual ordered field ℝ; entries are nonzero units.
proofSteps: Define D_n as a generated subgroup, not as a chosen unspecified complement. Expand each unit as its sign times its positive absolute value; multilinearity writes each symbol as an all-minus-one term plus terms with a positive entry.
The all-negative test is multiplicative in each entry. Complementary real numbers cannot both be negative, so it annihilates the Steinberg relation and gives the stated additive sign map.
Since −1 has square one, 2e_n=0; its sign is 1, so its order is exactly two. The expansion and sign calculation identify ker(sign)=D_n and prove directness of the sum.

For each m>0, a positive real entry has a positive mth root. Replacing that slot by its root yields an m-preimage still in D_n. Finite signed sums of generators inherit such preimages, so D_n is divisible.
In degree two transfer through degreeTwoEquiv. No assertion of unique divisibility of D_n is needed for this target.
acceptance: D₁ is the multiplicative positive reals written additively; sign gives ℝ×/D₁≅ℤ/2.
The pure all-minus-one symbol is outside D_n.
Degree zero is excluded: K⁽M⁾₀(ℝ)=ℤ.

sources.locator: Example III.7.2(c), printed pp.61–62; real symbol in Example III.6.2.1, printed pp.49–50
sources.match: The source identifies a sign summand and a divisible complement. Positive-entry generators give a canonical complement and a direct proof of its divisibility.

nodes.title: The cyclic-unit symbol annihilator
nodes.statement: Suppose F× is cyclic with generator g and c:F××F×→A is a bilinear Steinberg pairing. If char F=2, or if there exist complementary units a,b whose exponents relative to g are both odd, then c(g,g)=0 and consequently c is identically zero. Every finite field satisfies one of these alternatives.
hypotheses: F a commutative field with cyclic units; c takes values in an abelian group and annihilates complementary units.
proofSteps: Bilinearity reduces every value to an integer multiple of z=c(g,g). Field-calculus gives 2z=0.
In characteristic two the square formula immediately gives z=0. In odd characteristic the square and nonsquare unit cosets have equal size (q−1)/2.
On F minus {0,1}, there are (q−1)/2 nonsquares and only (q−3)/2 squares. If every nonsquare a had square 1−a, the involution a↦1−a would inject the larger set into the smaller, a contradiction.
Choose the resulting complementary nonsquares g^r,g^s with r,s odd. The Steinberg relation yields rsz=0; Bézout with the odd integer rs and 2 gives z=0.

Use the pinned cyclicity theorem for finite units. This proves the inherited Milnor finite-field vanishing without Matsumoto; the classical stable kernel still needs the separate finite-field presentation proof.
acceptance: For q=3 take a=b=−1; the relation directly kills z.
For q=2 normalization alone kills the symbol.
This argument does not assert that all finite-field stable K₂ is symbol-generated without a proof.

sources.locator: Corollary III.6.1.1, printed p.48; Example III.7.2(a), printed p.61
sources.match: The finite-field counting argument kills the universal bilinear Steinberg pairing. Separating it from classical symbol generation prevents a circular finite-field comparison.

Coordinate uniqueness means uniqueness of v, not uniqueness of unrestricted two unipotent factors. Retain determinant-one monomial signs. gaps.title: G-Bass-Tate: arithmetic high-degree proof remains unread
gaps.detail: Weibel Example III.7.2(a),(d), printed pp.61–62, states the Bass–Tate answers but does not prove them. The original Bass–Tate article, The Milnor ring of a global field, LNM342 (1973), pp.349–446, was not obtained from a freely readable primary copy or the cleared library. sourceIssues.locator: Exercise III.5.9, printed p.46/PDF page46, author-hosted separate Chapter III PDF (metadata creation 2012-10-10); scoped to this author copy only
sourceIssues.printed: The exercise identifies the commutator symbol with h(rs)h(s)⁻¹h(r)⁻¹.
sourceIssues.correction: With {r,s}=[h_ij(r),h_ik(s)] and commutator aba⁻¹b⁻¹, use h(rs)h(r)⁻¹h(s)⁻¹, equivalently h(r)h(s)h(rs)⁻¹. The printed expression is the inverse symbol.
sourceIssues.reason: Conjugation by h_ik(r) sends w_ij(s)w_ij(−1) to w_ij(rs)w_ij(−r), hence its commutator with h_ij(s) is h(rs)h(r)⁻¹h(s)⁻¹={r,s}. Skew-symmetry and swapping r,s give the equivalent torus cocycle. Matsumoto Lemma5.4(c), p26, independently gives the same positive cocycle for roots e_i−e_j and e_i−e_k whose Cartan pairing is +1. Same-root h(r),h(s) need not commute. As a concrete distinction, Weibel LemmaIII6.3 (printed p51) normalizes the t-adic tame symbol on Q(t) by ∂{t,2}=2; the inverse class maps to1/2, so the reversed expression is not merely an equal 2-torsion class.
